name: Protein Power diet

lead: Protein Power is a low-carbohydrate, high-protein diet created by physicians Michael R. Eades and Mary Dan Eades and popularised by their 1996 book of the same name. Its appearance payoff is fat loss: by cutting carbohydrates it aims to reduce insulin and the fat storage the authors attribute to it, leading to a leaner body.

The plan centres on animal foods such as red meat and eggs and limits foods like beans and whole grains. Critics, including nutrition writers and a 2001 American Heart Association committee statement, raised concerns about long-term health effects; supporters say it supports weight loss and better fitness.

paras: Followers build meals around meat, eggs and other protein foods and limit carbohydrate-rich foods. On bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, related low-carb and ketogenic eating is discussed by lifters for cutting body fat while training; posters debate details such as whether protein interferes with ketosis.

Wikipedia reports that the diet is high in saturated and total fat, low in calcium and can cause ketosis, poor stamina and kidney strain, with side effects including bad breath, constipation, fatigue and nausea. The AHA advised against high-protein diets in 2001, and people with chronic kidney disease are advised to avoid them.

angle.text: Followers use the plan to lose body fat, which makes muscle definition and facial leanness more visible. Critics attribute weight loss on such diets to calorie restriction.

lead: Protein Power is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet created by physicians Michael R. Eades and Mary Dan Eades and promoted in their book Protein Power, first published in 1996. [1]

For appearance, its aim is a leaner body through fat loss. The authors' premise is that reducing carbohydrate lowers insulin, which they say governs fat storage, and the book promises weight loss, fitness and health improvements within weeks. [1]

Critics describe it as a fad diet and say its claims have not been scientifically demonstrated; nutrition bodies have cautioned about long-term high-protein, high-fat low-carb eating. Lifters on bodybuilding forums discuss similar low-carb, high-protein approaches for cutting. [1][2]

paras: Protein Power is an animal-based eating plan centred on red meat and eggs that restricts carbohydrate-rich foods including beans and whole grains. Its central claim is that lowering carbohydrate lowers insulin, which controls fat storage, and so produces weight loss and better health. [1]

Nutritionists Fredrick J. Stare and Elizabeth Whelan called the diet too lopsided to be healthful. In 2001 the American Heart Association's Nutrition Committee strongly advised against high-protein diets, including this one, citing health risks and a lack of long-term studies. [1]

Critics describe the diet as high in saturated and total fat and low in calcium, associated with ketosis, poor stamina and kidney strain, and possibly with greater risk of heart disease, cancer and osteoporosis. Reported side effects include bad breath, constipation, fatigue and nausea. They say weight loss is likely temporary and results from calorie restriction. Experts advise people with chronic kidney disease to avoid it. [1]

The diet is not a core looksmaxxing topic. On T Nation, lifters discuss low-carb and ketogenic eating while cutting. One poster argued that protein does not knock a person out of ketosis, contrary to what he called orthodox keto views. [2]
No studies found on Protein Power specifically. Researchers have studied low-carbohydrate and high-protein diets more generally, and the AHA statement noted a lack of long-term data. [1]
